This pictures the return of Christ, gathering the elect from the four corners of the world. Jesus descends with a shout. We who are His hear His voice, and Rise up, and come away with Him.

*For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone;* it is spring. The rains fall and the flowers burst forth, and a time of peace is at hand. The signs of the season are showing. The fig tree puts forth her green figs.

**Matthew 24:32–33**
*Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh: So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors.*

She begs to see her love, he is among the clefts of the rock, the stairs of the mountains, as a dove, his face is upon those that take shelter from His wrath there. They fear him. But she longs to see him.

**Revelation 6:15–17**
*And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?*

*Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.* The wrath is upon these "little foxes," the wicked, those that spoil and corrupt the tender grapes. The wicked that seek to destroy the believers, especially during the great tribulation.

Her certainty of their love, that he is hers and she is his, even as he waits for his time, reflects the eternal security we have as believers in Christ. Waiting patiently for His return, when the day breaks and the shadows flee the light.

teachings.title: I am black, but comely: Christ and His beloved
teachings.summary: The Song pictures Christ and the saved: blackened by sin and servitude, yet made upright by His imputed righteousness and called fairest among women.
teachings.text:
We are in the penultimate book of the Bible for the purposes of my goal to write out studies of every book of the Bible. Only Song of Songs and Psalms remain.

Here in the first chapter of Solomon's ode to his love, we can observe why it is in scripture; the clear allegory of Christ and His beloved, the saved.

The poetic language used, going back and forth between the woman and the man, is beautiful prose in itself. Begging for kisses from one whose love is better than wine. Whose savour is as good ointments.

The use of ointment and fine, perfumed oils as a representation of the Spirit, is found throughout the Bible. Her saying that even the king's name is as an ointment poured forth, that the virgins, or the innocent ladies in wait, do love him. Just as the righteous in Christ love even the name of Jesus.

She says to draw them, the damsels, to call them. And they will run after him. Just as the Spirit calls us, as a sweet savour to those that seek Him, calls us, and we willingly respond. *We will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.*

The upright, like virgin, indicates the quality of the saved. We are the righteousness of God. We have Jesus imputed righteousness upon us and a new man within, making us as virgins in His eyes. The forgiveness of the Father. We are upright because He is upright, and we are His.

 *I am black, but comely*...the woman isn't referring to race here, but the darkness of her skin from the sun. Her mother's children were angry with her, forcing her to keep their vineyards and to feed the sheep.

But the blackness is also sin, what it does to our heart. And the daughters are unbelieving Israel. They who persecuted the prophets and would crucify Christ. The world hates believers, because of His love for us. That despite our sin and being made their servants to do the work of the field, He so loves us.

The bride, having spoken of her love, and having told the daughters of Jerusalem her unworthiness, and having sought to find the king, hears back from him.

She seeks out his flocks, to be with him, and Solomon responds to her in verse 8. *If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents.*

He praises her, after her own shameful confession. She calls herself black from the work of being a servant. He calls her most fair among women. This is how Christ views His own.

Solomon says, follow the footsteps of the flock. Find the shepherds. We are Jesus' sheep. He is our Good Shepherd. We may find Him where the other sheep are, and follow in their footsteps that we may know Him.

Solomon goes on to describe his beloved in epic terms, and the chorus of the daughters of Jerusalem tells of how they will dress her in fine jewels and ornaments of fine gold and silver as the King's desire. Where before the children of Israel had despised her, the fair daughters of Jerusalem follow the lead of the King, and honor who he has chosen.

Verse 12 sees the woman at the King's table. In his court. The spiced wine calls him. She compares her attraction to him as the pleasant smell of myrrh, and her desire is for him to lay upon her bosom all night.

He is like a cluster of henna flowers, or *camphire*, alluring, heavily scented clusters of small white and yellow flowers used as perfume.

She longs for him, his eyes like a doves. Their bed green. The beams cedar and rafters fir. The finest materials build their house, and she wishes to live with him forever.

teachings.title: A godly seed: the promise was always Christ
teachings.summary: The godly seed God sought is Christ, the singular seed of Abraham, and Israel's marriage covenant ended when they slew their Husband.
teachings.text:
Malachi, the last prophet before the days of the coming of Christ, continues to preach the word of God against the Jews.

First Levi and her priests, then Judah and her foreign brides. Their iniquity and calling evil good and good evil.

Their table has become a snare.

Their adultery is to the covenant God made with their fathers, and to Him. And here, in Malachi 2:15, we see the reason behind the covenant, the Old Testament given to Moses in the wilderness. That He may seek a godly seed.

While some will say this is about Israel, it is, like God's promise to Abraham, seed singular. As of one.

**Galatians 3:16-17**
*Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect.*

The promise was always Christ.

*And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed.*

This was always the gospel. This was always the promise. The good news.

And the fault for the first testament ending was with the people. The Lord hates putting away. And so in death, their marriage was ended, even the death of Christ.

The law says *The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead*.

They slew their Husband, and hung Him on a tree.

teachings.title: Hephzibah and Beulah, the bride
teachings.summary: The bride married to the Lord is the New Jerusalem, and Judah was spared only for David's promise and the place of His name, never for the Jews themselves.
teachings.text:
**Isaiah 62** is a love letter from the Lord for the city of Jerusalem, the mountains of Zion, the land where God chooses to place His holy name.

The valleys and the mountains made straight, and level for the King's Highway. The path of the King.

*Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah* (the delight of), *and thy land Beulah* (the bride*): for the Lord delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married.*

This again calls forward to the events described in **Revelation 21**, which I posted yesterday. The New Jerusalem that depends from Heaven, decked as a bride.

People often talk about the wedding of the church to Christ. I know it's used as parable a couple times, but the actual feast is here and the bride that golden city, where Christ will reign forever.

We've seen it again and again in the Chronicles and Kings, and from the prophets, that the only reason Judah wasn't destroyed like Sodom, like Israel, was the promise to David, that the Christ promised to Abraham would come from the King's lineage. And, every time, to keep Jerusalem as the place God chose to place His name. As the spot where Jesus would be offered. And where He would triumphantly reign.

It was never the Jews. They were beneficiaries of God's plan. They were not His plan, themselves.

And when the city was made desolate by the captivity, the exile to Babylon. And, in the Great Tribulation, when the abomination of desolation is made, when many would say that Jerusalem is "Forsaken," that it will not be. That Christ's redeemed will flock to Jerusalem, a crown of glory. A royal diadem. The symbol of His power.

teachings.title: Hosea buys back the adulteress
teachings.summary: Hosea's redeeming an adulteress pictures God expecting faithfulness from Israel through desolation, because in the latter days they would seek the Lord and David their king, who is Christ.
teachings.text:
Here again, the Lord instructed the prophet to play the cuckold, to love a woman as a friend who is an adulteress, just as Israel played the harlot to their God.

The Lord is that man, the people wickedly left His protection and provision for wine and idols, as an unfaithful wife.

Hosea purchases the service of a whore for a pittance, (15 pieces of silver is half the 30 that is the price of a servant, a measure and a half of barley, barely enough for bread), but with the expectation of faithfulness, to represent the desolation that is to come upon Israel and Judah. A time where the plenty of God is taken away. No king, no sacrifice, no priestly duties, no image to bow to. And yet He wants them to know by this preaching that the Lord expects them to suffer through this loss and still maintain their faithfulness to Him. Something they weren't able to do in plenty, now do in tribulation.

But why? Because of the promise of the Lord, that in the latter end of things, they will seek the Lord their God and David their king, being Christ Jesus, and receive His goodness once again.

teachings.title: A door of hope: Ishi, not Baali
teachings.summary: Hosea's door of hope in the valley of Achor is Christ the door, and calling God Ishi (husband) rather than Baali promises the close relationship we have in Christ.
teachings.text:
*Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah.* **Hosea 2** opens with the word of the Lord coming to the prophet, to appeal to the men of Israel as brothers, or "my people," to the women saying "the one who is loved," those to whom God has shown mercy. God reminding them of why He feels as He does towards them; that they understand their whoredoms and the wrath that has come about because of their worship of Baalim.

The Lord compares them again to an unfaithful wife, who has run off with different lovers, who credits the wealth and plenty they have to these strange gods. And now He would strip them bare, leaving the nation desolate because of them.

The Lord then gives Hosea prophecy, that from the wilderness He will give to His people vineyards, and a door of hope in the valley of trouble. (Achor, meaning "trouble," being the valley near Jericho, where Achan was swallowed up by the Lord for disobedience). Wild vines, given as God's people, and rescued from trouble, or tribulation. Given a door of hope, Christ Jesus:

**John 10:9**
 *I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture*.

And in that day, says the Lord, thou (meaning His people), shall call Him "*Ishi*," that is husband, rather than "*Baali*," that is "Lord." A promise of a closer, personal relationship with God that we have in Christ.

Blotting out the names of the false lords, the gods of the heathen, that only one name under Heaven be praised.

And God promises again the peace to come, the perfect Kingdom of Heaven. Where the tools of war are broken, and even the beasts of creation live in peace.

**Isaiah 11:6-9**
*The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them. And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.*

teachings.title: The law could not redeem, Boaz could
teachings.summary: The nearer kinsman pictures the law, able to keep land but not redeem the person, while Boaz pictures Christ, who redeems us and raises the dead to their inheritance.
teachings.text:
The laws of the right of redemption, and the process of securing a means of redeeming a property to keep it as part of the inheritance of the extended family, and more importantly, the redemption of the childless widow, to keep the dead man's name, to raise the dead to its inheritance, are a like picture of Christ.

In this case, you see the nearer kinsman offered the right to redeem the parcel of land, and his willingness to do so, but his inability to redeem the person, Ruth, and raise the name of the dead. This is a picture of the Law itself.

By the Law the people could maintain their land, to keep the inheritance within the family. But the Law is unable to redeem the person, and raise their name from the dead unto their inheritance.

Boaz, picturing Christ Jesus, desires to, and is able, to do both.

And Ruth, a figure of the believer who has called upon the Lord to save her, bearing fruit and building up Israel, the Israel of God, that are other believers.

It was a shame for the nearest kin to refuse redemption. The widow would remove the shoe of the man who rejected the right, and spit in his face before the people. Here, because of the amicable arrangement and willingness of Boaz, the man simply removes his shoe, to show he is less worthy than the son of Judah who has fufiled the role.

Similarly, John the Baptist, when speaking of the Messiah, said of his cousin, Jesus;

**John 1:26-27**
*John answered them, saying, I baptize with water: but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not;*
*he it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose.*

Just as water baptism had no power to regenerate the dead - to rise them up that their name not be blotted out of Israel, unto their inheritance, redeemed - but Christ could. John says he is not worthy to even loosen the laces of Jesus' shoe.

In a like manner the law was incapable of redemption, but by Jesus we are bought. We are paid for with a price. We are redeemed.

teachings.title: Spread thy skirt over thine handmaid
teachings.summary: Ruth at Boaz's feet pictures the believer calling on Christ, our near kinsman, to cover and protect us.
teachings.text:
Naomi tells Ruth she seeks rest for her. That the lord is at work that night, on the threshing floor. Winnowing wheat from chaff. She instructs Ruth to go in an find where he shall lie and uncover his feet and lay down before him, and the lord will tell her what to do.

The picture of salvation and redemption in Christ is wonderful.

Boaz eats and drinks, and merrily lays down from his labors on the heaps of barley corn, and sleeps. Ruth enters and uncovers his feet and laid down. At midnight, Boaz wakes startled at the woman at his feet and asks who it is.

And Ruth asks Boaz to "spread his skirt" over her, his handmaid. To cover her in his protection, because he is a near kinsman.

She calls upon the lord. Just as we ask the Lord Christ Jesus to protect us. To gather us under his wing as a hen does her chicks. Because He is God made flesh, a Son of man, our near kinsman.

teachings.title: Myrrh, aloes and cassia on the King
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: The spices on the King's garments in Psalm 45 picture the gospel: myrrh His sacrificial death, aloes His incorruption and resurrection, and cassia His ascension and eternal priesthood.
teachings.text:
The anointing oil is based on olive oil, but contains the other spices for fragrance, myrrh and cassia.

**Exodus 30:22–29**
*Moreover the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels, And of cassia five hundred shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, and of oil olive an hin: And thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil. And thou shalt anoint the tabernacle of the congregation therewith, and the ark of the testimony, And the table and all his vessels, and the candlestick and his vessels, and the altar of incense, And the altar of burnt offering with all his vessels, and the laver and his foot. And thou shalt sanctify them, that they may be most holy: whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy.*

This ointment is given of God to sanctify, and make all that it is applied to, holy. But it was reserved for the items of the Tabernacle and the High Priest, a holy anointing oil.

**Exodus 30:32**
*Upon man’s flesh shall it not be poured, neither shall ye make any other like it, after the composition of it: it is holy, and it shall be holy unto you.*

God also instructed not to anoint a stranger with this, as it is holy, threatening to cut off any who do it from the people.

Yet it is this holy oil, reserved for the things of God and His High Priest, that is given to the King described in **Psalm 45**.

Myrrh is a bitter resin extracted from a thorny tree, that was primarily used in burial preparations. It was given as a gift for a King by the wisemen visiting the infant Jesus.

Nicodemus used myrrh and aloes in the preparation of the body of Christ at His burial.

**John 19:39–40**
*And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight. Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.*

There is a sense of the suffering of Christ, the death He tasted for all men, in the application of myrrh in the Psalm, reflected in the Gospels.

The scent of myrrh on the King carries with it His majesty, that cannot be separated from His sacrificial death. His garments carry the scent of His ultimate act of love.

The aloes mentioned are not the oil we know today, but the fragrance made from an eaglewood tree, and those aloes are found in Nicodemus' mixture. Because aloes were used to preserve bodies and counteract the smell of decay, they symbolize resurrection, healing, and incorruptibility of Christ, in His death.

**Psalms 16:10**
*For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.*

Cassia is an aromatic bark, like cinnamon, and is used in the holy anointing oil, mentioned above. This ties in to the understanding of Christ not only as King but High Priest.

Taken together, these three spices combined on the garments of the King paint a complete picture of the Gospel narrative. Myrrh as the sacrificial death, aloes His incorruption and resurrection, and cassia, Jesus' ascension, and role as High Priest, forever.

And so in **Psalm 45**, as the King approaches His bride, He carries with Him the literal aroma of redemption. The scent of His gospel. Amen

teachings.title: Why do the heathen rage
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Psalm 2 prophesies the rulers' vain rebellion against God's anointed, whom God raised up and set as King over the nations, warning rulers to kiss the Son and trust in Him.
teachings.text:
Why do the heathen rage? Why do people think they can go against God? Kings and rulers, presidents and prime ministers, popes and priests, all seek to be freed from the ways of the Lord, to do what they will.

Especially the religious and political leaders in the time of Jesus.

**Acts 4:27**
*For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together*.

They believed if they killed the Son, they would break the bands, Their bonds, and be free of God.

Jesus addressed this in a parable, about a Lord who planted a vineyard and lent it out to husbandmen to dress and keep it. And when the Lord sent servants to gather the harvest, the stewards beat and killed them. So finally, the Lord sends his son;

**Matthew 21:38**
*But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance*.

David prophetically writes of this here in **Psalm 2**.

But, it is folly. The Lord holds them in derision. He laughs at their vain efforts, because Christ, His anointed, rose again.

He set His Son upon Zion, and upon the throne.

**Acts 13:32–33**
*And we declare unto you glad tidings, how that the promise which was made unto the fathers, God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.*

Jesus' inheritance are all the nations of the world, and possession of the uttermost parts of the world. And as Lord of lords and King of kings, He will rule them.

**Revelation 2:26–27**
*And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations: And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father.*

This prophetic Psalm gives warning to the rulers of this world, reminding them of their place. That they serve at the pleasure of the Lord, and He will deliver vengeance.

It's an amazing and consistent message, across the entire Bible; The Christ is God's anointed, and Jesus is the Christ. All who believe on Christ Jesus shall be saved. His grace and mercy giving us the chance to serve Him in righteousness.

*Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.*

Amen

teachings.title: The Branch, a priest upon His throne
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Joshua's crowning prophesies the Branch, Christ, who is both King and High Priest after the order of Melchizedek.
teachings.text:
Then Zechariah is given the word of the Lord saying to him to gather 3 men, who had been taken into captivity, and bring them out of Babylon to go to the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah, and there make Joshua the high priest of the Levites crowns, and set them upon his head and deliver this prophecy:

*Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, saying, Behold the man whose name is* The Branch*; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the Lord: Even he shall build the temple of the Lord; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.*

This is a prophecy of Christ, both King and High Priest. The term "The Branch" is a messianic title used elsewhere in the Old Testament, such as **Isaiah 11:1** *And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots* and **Jeremiah 23:5** *I will raise unto David a righteous* Branch*, and a King shall reign and prosper*. This signifies a descendant of David, pointing to the Messiah being a son of David.

The dual role of Jesus in being both King and Priest is referenced in **Hebrews 7:11-28**, where Jesus is described as a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who was both king of Salem and high priest.

teachings.title: The covenant of salt: true King and true Priest
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: The covenants of salt with the Levites and with David contrast the true king and priesthood with Jeroboam's counterfeit, picturing Christ as King and High Priest against the beast and false prophet.
teachings.text:
Here in **2 Chronicles 13**, we are given the story of the short-lived reign of King Abijah, son of Jeroboam. He reigned 3 years, and in that time Rehoboam King of Israel rose up an army to spoil Judah.

In the depiction given by the chronicler, he stood mighty upon mount Zenaraim in Ephraim, with 400,000 valiant men, while Rehoboam met him with twice as many, and surrounded his forces by ambush.

But King Abijah, standing defiantly calls upon the name of the Lord, and reminds us of the thing by which Jeroboam caused all Israel to sin; turning from the Lord, building golden calves to worship, casting out the priests of Aaron, and the Levites whom God gave a covenant of salt to;

**Numbers 18:19**
*All the heave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer unto the LORD, have I given thee, and thy sons and thy daughters with thee, by a statute for ever: it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD unto thee and to thy seed with thee*.

And reminds us that God's covenant with David is also a covenant of salt;

*Ought ye not to know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?*

These are the only two appearances of the term, and it is given that these two covenants are preserved like as by salt, in perpetuity.

Contrasting with Jeroboam, a false king, and his priesthood, made up of baser men of the lewd sort, where anyone who could bring a young bullock and 7 rams could buy their way in.

The true King and true Priest vs the false, the counterfeit. Very much a picture of Christ Jesus, Who is both King and High Priest, forever vs the beast and his antichrist, and their false prophet.

Abijah gives a good accounting of faithful Judah and the Levitical ceremony and sacrifices kept as God had given them, fundamentalist, the Old Paths, vs these modernist perversions and Idolatry.

The Lord is with the armies of Abijah, and they slay 500K Israelites, routing them and taking Bethel and other lands from the North.

teachings.title: Mephibosheth at the king's table
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Mephibosheth, crippled and spared to eat at the king's table, pictures the sinner given grace by Christ, and we are to show others the same mercy.
teachings.text:
Here in **2 Samuel 9**, we see David, now King of Israel, honoring the covenant made with Jonathan, the son of Saul. He extends not only mercy and forgiveness to Mephibosheth, but provides him with his inheritance, servants to care for him, and that he shall eat at the king's table, forever.

Mephibosheth is a picture of a sinner, seeking grace in the eyes of the King, who is a picture of Christ. He was crippled in youth, as we are in sin, and custom would have the heirs of the previous king killed, yet David not only pardons him that fate, but sets him up as an adopted son, welcome at his table.

This is the mercy and grace we are to show to people. David, unlike the paranoid Saul, does this kindness and keeps his oath and is rewarded by the loyalty of Mephibosheth later during an uprising, when the young lord is betrayed by the servant, Ziba, who David had placed under him.

(Ziba is a picture of the Jews who were unfaithful servants, as we will see in chapter 19)

The world today would see David's actions as weak and foolish, but as we see again and again his faith in the Lord and willingness to forgive and make peace has led to David being strong, bringing the whole region under his control. Blessed by God, his enemies destroyed before him.

This lesson, to be as David, to show the mercy and grace God showed us on others, is a lesson in faith.

teachings.title: The giant-slayer's reward and our liberty
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: The king's promised reward for slaying Goliath pictures what Christ gives by faith: eternal life, sonship and freedom from the wages of sin.
teachings.text:
And so the future king, David, confronts the Philistine champion, and with his faith, slays the giant with one blow. And using Goliath's own sword, slays him and decapitates him. The Philistines flee, the emboldened Israelites pursue and slaughter them and spoil their camp.

David returns to the king, with the trophy of his victory with him.

Earlier in the story, when David learned of Goliath, the men of the camp had rumoured that whosoever slay the giant would be rewarded by the king;

*Have ye seen this man that is come up? surely to defy Israel is he come up: and it shall be, that the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel.*

This is a picture of the victory Christ gives us, the reward we are elected into for allowing God to deliver us in Him, by faith. We are rewarded with eternal life, and are made His sons. And we become free, that is are set at liberty. In David's case, the family of Jesse would live tax free in the kingdom. In ours, we live free of the tax on our sin, the wages of death.

And so with the victory won, David brought the head of the giant to Jerusalem, but kept the armor as spoil.

Saul, as he sent off David, asks his captain of the host, Abner, *whose son is this youth?* Abner doesn't know but seeks to find out. Saul, who had known David, been soothed by the boy's harp and psalms, who had offered to bear his armor, hadn't bothered to know anything of him.

After the fact, Abner brings David and his trophy before the king, who asks "whose son are you?" David answered Jesse of Bethlehem, but this is a picture of Jesus Christ. There's an echo of Jesus being brought before Herod, accused of the Jews for saying truthfully that He was the son of God.

teachings.title: A man after God's own heart
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Saul's unlawful sacrifice cost him the kingdom, while David, the man after God's heart, foreshadows Christ who is both King of kings and an acceptable High Priest forever.
teachings.text:
**1 Samuel 13** is part one of a story regarding a particular battle with the Philistines, introducing Jonathan, King Saul's son, a faithful believer and mighty man of valor. It also continues to establish Saul as having questionable judgement when it comes to certain decisions, especially here in chapter 13. Decisions that have long lasting ramifications.

There are skirmishes with the Philistine garrisons and spoilers, or raiding parties, had been plaguing Israel. Saul with his 2,000 men and Jonathan with a thousand had gone against them and smote some, and the Philistines gathered to fight with 30,000 chariots and 6,000 horsemen and people as the sand which is on the sea shore. Their occupation has brought with it abomination in the land.

And the people of Israel his themselves from this fierce army. In rocks and caves and thickets of wood. Some fled to Gad over Jordan.

And Saul remained with his men, who were afraid. And Samuel had instructed Saul, telling the king to tarry 7 days for him that he would make an offering unto the Lord. But, the king, impatient at Samuel being late, and seeing the people scattered and afraid decided to wait no longer. He took it up on himself to do burnt offerings to the Lord.

As he does, Samuel arrives and Saul goes to greet him. Samuel asks, What have you done?

*Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash; Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the Lord: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.*

Samuel rebukes the king, saying;
*Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever. But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the Lord commanded thee.*

Spoilers; we know this man after God's own heart is David.

**Acts 13:21-22**
*And afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave their testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.*

This also is a prophecy of Christ Jesus, who, like David would fulfil all the Father's will.

And unlike Saul, Jesus is both King of kings, but also a high priest, forever. And unlike Saul His sacrifice being as the Father had ordained, and fully acceptable.

**Hebrews 4:14-16**
*Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.*

And so Saul in his haste, acting as a priest and not king, showed in his zeal a lack of judgement and faith. And sowed further seeds of his own destruction.

teachings.title: The Levites' portion and Christ our High Priest
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: The Levitical covenant pictures Christ our only High Priest, which Jews no longer have, and the Levites' lack of land pictures our separation from this world.
teachings.text:
Here in **Numbers 18**, following the budding of Aaron's rod in the previous chapter, we have God's covenant with the Levites and Aaron and his sons, and their portion. The Levitical priesthood is given to them the service of the Tabernacle, and the iniquity of the people to be cleansed in offerings as an ordinance of the faith. And Aaron and his sons to take their iniquity and those of the Levites, and make offerings unto the Lord.

The Lord gives them the gift of service and in exchange they will live off their portion of the meats given to the Lord, the tithes taken, which the priests offer up a tenth themselves. And they are set to redeem the firstborn with the shekels commanded of God after the deaths of the firstborn of Egypt, at Passover.

These Levitical laws are given as a picture of Christ to come and the service of the Lord that Christians today are called to. To offer redemption and forgiveness to the people.

It is funny that of all the talk of covenants by dispensationalists, they never bring this one up. As so-called Jews have no priesthood. No offerings. No cleansing of the iniquity and trespass and sin of the people. No redemption of the first born. No heave offering. No sacrifice for their atonement.

The admonishments against allowing non-Levites into the Tabernacle, and even against Levites entering behind the veil which was for Aaron and his sons, that those who offended would surely die, is again showing there is only one way to please God, by following His word. It echoes the commandment given Adam in the garden. It is repeated in Christ's preaching that He is the only way to the Father. Our High Priest.

The lack of an inheritance in the land, among the children of Israel, other than service, is a like picture of the separation we as Christians should have with this world. We look towards a better country. A heavenly Kingdom. We are a holy nation. A peculiar people. A royal priesthood. The cares of this world are not ours. But the service of the Lord, and the blessings that come from it are our portion. As the increase of the threshing floor. As the increase of the winepress. Amen

teachings.title: The covenant of salt
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: The covenant of salt given to Aaron's priesthood and David's kingdom is fulfilled in Christ, and believers are the salt that preserves the world.

teachings.title: Aaron's rod that budded
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Aaron's dead rod that budded pictures Christ, the risen Branch and our High Priest, whom men resent and rebel against today.
teachings.text:
The budding of Aaron's rod, a dead branch, brought to life, as an image of the chosen High Priest of the people is a clear and obvious picture of Christ Jesus. A rod out of the stem of Jesse, a Branch that grew out of his roots. Who was dead and was risen, and, like the almonds that Aaron's rod brought forth, Jesus gave forth fruit for all time, those that believe on His holy name.

Aaron's rod is added to the Ark with the manna and the tablets, in the Tabernacle of testimony. They literally were carrying God's word made manifest, in the heart of their camp. The testimony that His word was true.

This method of quelling rebellion amongst the children of Israel, allowing the will of God to be made clear by way of miracle, seems to us perfectly decisive. Aaron would be the high priest. The Levites would serve the Tabernacle. A gift to the Lord, given to bear the iniquity of the people. And to redeem them. As the next chapter tells us;

*And ye shall keep the charge of the sanctuary, and the charge of the altar: that there be no wrath any more upon the children of Israel.*

And Moses did as the Lord commanded him.

But did the anointing of Aaron and his sons and the Levites cease the murmurings of the children of Israel?

*And the children of Israel spake unto Moses, saying, Behold, we die, we perish, we all perish. Whosoever cometh any thing near unto the tabernacle of the Lord shall die: shall we be consumed with dying?*

They acknowledged that they would perish if they came near the Tabernacle. That there would be only the Levitical priesthood as God commands, but their fear of dying makes them seem bitter.

Their understanding that they shall all perish without accepting the rod that God had chosen to bear their iniquity, who would redeem them, coupled with fear, carries with it a resentment that mirrors that of people today, reacting to the truth of Christ Jesus as our high priest. A resentment that in many hearts leads to rebellion and reprobation.

God's word doesn't just provide us the model of faith and sanctification that we see in men like Moses, or Caleb. Or as we will see in Joshua. Scripture seems to show us more glimpses of unbelief in stiff-necked and gainsaying people. And the destruction they suffer as a result of their pride.

But we are those who hear God's word, see the budding of the rod and know His will, and delight in it. Or we should if we walk in the Spirit, reading His word. That we gain understanding and acceptance of it. Amen

teachings.title: The veil rent: come boldly to the throne
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: The high priest entered behind the veil only once a year, but Christ's death rent the veil, so believers may come boldly before God at any time through Christ our high priest.
teachings.text:
Now to the narrative of events, following the deaths of Aaron's sons, God provided Aaron with an assurance that if he came before the presence of God, beyond the veil, under the ceremonial ordinances laid out; his sin offering, the linen robes and mitre that were holy, his washings, etc, that the Lord promises he will not be struck down as well. Remember, their sin was in adding to the ordinances their own doctrine, using strange fire and not the fire the Lord has provided.

And so the high priest would only enter the holy place, behind the veil, once a year to fulfill these sacrifices of atonement, first for himself and then all the people.

But when Christ had died, that veil was torn. As told by Matthew:

*And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent*...

And as Paul wrote of the veil and the unbelieving Jews:

2 Corinthians 3:14-18
*but their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ. But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart. Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.*

And so we know we may go before the Lord boldly, and at any time, because Christ is our high priest;

**Hebrews 4:14-16**
*Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.*

Because we have been made heirs, the sons of God and given access to the Lord by His grace and mercy, through faith in His Son;

**Ephesians 2:6**
*And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus*

For God is not slack concerning His promises.

**1 John 1:9**
 *If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.*

teachings.title: A Priest After the Order of Melchisedec
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Christ is a High Priest after the order of Melchisedec, greater than Levi, and the change of priesthood disannulled the law of Moses.
teachings.text:
And so, having established Jesus Christ's nature and purpose and the order of things pertaining to salvation of grace, including the rejection of the Gospel of truth, Paul returns again to his thesis, directed at the believing Hebrews, that Jesus is our High Priest, after the order of Melchisedec. Different than the order of Aaron. Separate from those Levite-born.

By necessity of a better testament and through the eternal life of Jesus, who was sinless and without spot, both the priest and the sacrifice, He is our High priest promised in the Psalms.

Paul is building the case that they who were under the law but now are saved by faith in Christ have no need of the human preists given by Moses, and the sacrifices and carnal ordinances are done away with in Jesus.

Some call this replacement theology, the replacement of the Jews as the "chosen people of God," with the Holy nation created from all tongues and kindreds by those who believe. But, as we see by Abram's tithing to Melchizedek, the High Priest of the most high God. Melchizedek who blessed Abram, *and without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better.*

The Levites are of Abraham. And in Abraham, paid tithes to the King of Peace. The ruler of Salem. The High Priest of God who is without beginning or end. Like unto the Son of God. The less paid honor to the greater.

This is an important concept for the early church, which had many raised as Jews. Paul is laying out the replacement. The disannulling of the law of Moses. *For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law.*

He reasons that the Levitical preists were made such without any oath by God, but the Spirit through David made such an oath regarding Jesus, that He be made a High Priest after the order of Melchisedek. Another promise made by God who cannot lie. To whom we have our full trust in, and see Jesus as the surety of the promise of eternal life, and so we must accept His vows given through His word. And the implications thereof are clear;

*But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself. For the law maketh men high priests which have infirmity; but the word of the oath, which was since the law, maketh the Son, who is consecrated for evermore.*

Amen!

teachings.title: Come Boldly to the Throne of Grace
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Because Christ is a High Priest tempted like us, believers go boldly to God through Him alone, with no need of saints, Mary or sacraments.
teachings.text:
*Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.*

Having established that Jesus is God, Who created all things but was made by the will of the Father a little lower than the angels, made flesh to suffer and die for our sins, we can know that we have a High Priest, an advocate, who isn't some lofty god uncaring of our foibles and weakness, but Who at all points was tempted as we are, and through Whom we may boldly enter before God, His throne of grace, seeking mercy and help in our times of need. With the knowledge that God understands and loves us. We may enter boldly because we have such a High Priest in Jesus, He is the only mediator between God and man. There is no other name under Heaven by which we may be saved. There is no work by our own hands which can save us. There is no doubt of our salvation to those that believe. We enter into His rest by heeding His word and believing it.

And so we see, there is no calling on a "saint," or "Mary" to intercede, to bring us salvation, or any works, rites or sacraments that saves us from death and Hell. There is only faith in God's word and His perfect work, done from the beginning. The Lamb slain before the foundation of the world.

teachings.title: Melchizedek, a picture of Christ
teachings.theme: Christ our King and High Priest
teachings.summary: Melchizedek, priest of the most high God with bread and wine and receiving tithes, pictures or is Christ, showing the patriarchs' faith was always about Jesus.
teachings.text:
As always, the New Testament is the best study guide for the Old Testament. Here Paul gives us understanding into who exactly Melchizedek king of Salem, priest of the most high God was, or at least pictures; Jesus Christ.

The appearance of Jesus throughout the OT, when the LORD speaks in person to the patriarchs, is called a "theophany," and most believers see Jesus in the "angel of God" passages throughout Genesis, the Lord who meets with and speaks to them, who appears to stop Abraham's hand sacrificing Issac, who wrestles with Jacob, appears in the fiery furnace in Daniel...Many such cases. As the Bible itself is one story, telling us about God, Jesus, the Holy Ghost and the Godhead's relationship with man, Jesus appears in every book of the Old Testament, regardless of manifestation.

And here, Melchizedek is seen as an early appearance of Jesus, taking tithes from Abraham, the king of peace, the preists of the high God. Without a beginning or end, no mother or father given, *made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually.*

And his use by Paul as an example of a non-Levitical priest, to whom tithes and honor are due, that he was a pattern of Jesus and the preisthood of believers of Christ Himself. Showing that the less was blessed by the greater, saying *Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth: And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand.* Melchizedek, *whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils.*

I believe it is Jesus, personally. But either way, it's a sign that the ordinance of bread and wine, of faith in God as savior, as the faith of the patriarchs, that it was always about Jesus.

teachings.title: Daniel saw a glorified Jesus
teachings.summary: The man in linen of Daniel 10 matches John's vision of Christ in Revelation 1, so he believes it was a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus.
teachings.text:
And so, the story picks up at the side of the Tigris River, Hiddekel as its called here. And there appears to him an angel with great wonder in his appearance. The others with Daniel do not see him, but a great quaking, or fear befell the other men and they fled.

Daniel describes the appearance of this messenger as wearing garments of linen and gold, his body like beryl, a crystalline or silicate mineral, like aquamarine and emeralds. His face had the appearance of lightening, his eyes as lamps of fire and his arms and feet as polished brass. His voice like the voice of a multitude.

I have heard people say this is Gabriel, but Daniel had already met that angel, and his appearance was as a man and did not cause the reaction this sight gives him. Daniel passes out in shock and struggles throughout to gain his composure.

The description reminds me of how Jesus is described in **Revelation 1**.

*And I turned to see the voice that spake with me. And being turned, I saw seven golden candlesticks; And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle. His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow; and his eyes were as a flame of fire; And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters. And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength. And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead.*

We see John has the same reaction as Daniel, and the description of linen and gold clothes, eyes as flame, feet the color of brass, a supernaturally loud voice...I believe Daniel was talking with a glorified Jesus. A Christophany, or pre-NT appearance of Jesus. But I am not dogmatic on that.

It would make His delay, striving against the prince of Persia, the evil spirit set in place over the government seem off, as God wouldn't need help of Michael the captain of the host, to deal with it. However, if this was a dispute between demonic principalities, and the influence on Cyrus to let the people go, it may well be that it was a battle to get the king to make a decision, to come to do the right thing, which he eventually did. A spiritual battle all men knowingly or unknowingly are a part of. Especially those who are chosen by God to be leaders.

**Ephesians 6:12**
*For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.*

teachings.title: The brazen serpent lifted up
teachings.summary: When Israel despised the manna God sent serpents, and the brazen serpent lifted up pictures Christ, that whosoever looks to Him should live.
teachings.text:
*And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread*.

Chapter 21 of Numbers begins with a military victory, God delivering their enemies into their hands, and it ends with military victories. And yet in the midst of it, we see this familiar complaint of the Israelites.

"If God be real, why bad stuff happen?" They are spoiled by their own lack of faith and gratitude.

They begin during their journey having spies captured in the land of Arad king of the Canaanites, and so the people bowing a vow to the Lord that they will utterly destroy the cities of their foes, if He delivers them into their hands.

And the Lord hears them and does just that, and they destroy the cities of the Canaanites. But this faith in Him is short lived. As they sought a way around Edom to avoid their borders, they become discouraged again. And complain again.

They say they have no water, despite being given water multiple times. They say they have no bread, despite even admitting it is the "light bread" of Manna that they are sick of.

And so the Lord sends fiery serpents among them to torment and slay the people of Israel. You would think they'd have learned this lesson, but people can be stubborn. Have short memories of what God has done for them. Don't appreciate blessings and come to despise the spiritual bread. A like picture of the word come down from Heaven. Daily reading of scripture is for the NT Christian the same as gathering the Manna, to grind into bread. They have backslidden and we tend to as well when we neglect that daily bread.

And so, His wrath revealed against them, they come to Moses to beg forgiveness. And the Lord tells him to make a brazen snake, that the people may look upon it lifted up, and live. A picture of Christ;

**John 3:14-16**
 *And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.*

teachings.title: Speak to the rock
teachings.summary: Speaking to the rock pictures calling upon Christ for living water, and Moses lost the promised land by striking it in disobedience.
teachings.text:
**Numbers 20** begins like most stories about the children of Israel, complaining and carrying on with a lack of faith or fear of the Lord.

They have witnessed triumphant miracles, seen the hand of the Lord strike down their enemies by the sea they passed through. Been guided through the desert by a pillar of flame. Had their bellies filled with bread made from manna of heaven. And have had water come from out from a rock to drink.

They have seen punishment of the Lord, His wrath revealed from Heaven, taking out thousands of their people. By fire. Plague. Venom. The earth swallowing up those that rebelled against the Lord.

His mercy and His wrath, the same revelations which Paul writes about in Romans, that no man has an excuse to not know and fear the Lord.

And yet they complain.

And so here, having been condemned for a generation to wander the wilderness for their unbelief in the promise of God to deliver them into the promised land, and fresh off of the rebellion that had the Lord had slain so many by plague, they once again complained to Moses. "Wherefore have ye made us to come up out of Egypt?" Lacking faith that God would provide.

Moses and Aaron go to the Lord in prayer with their problem. The correct thing to do, of course.

*And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Take the rod, and gather thou the assembly together, thou, and Aaron thy brother, and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes; and it shall give forth his water, and thou shalt bring forth to them water out of the rock: so thou shalt give the congregation and their beasts drink.*

Similar to the event that happened earlier in Exodus, the people murmuring in complaint, and God had Moses strike the rock and brought forth water. So the people knew it was possible and Moses knew to follow the word of the Lord. And yet, in his anger or frustration, Moses disobeyed the word of God, and instead of speaking to the rock, he struck it with his rod. Not once, as at *Meribah* in Exodus, but twice.

Speaking to the rock is a picture of calling upon Christ for salvation; *If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.* God wishes to be sanctified by the people from this miracle. (Not that He needs man to make him holy, in this use it means to acknowledge that He is holy.)

And because Moses disobeyed His word, God keeps Him and Aaron from ever stepping foot in the land He had promised them.

But the water came forth and the people and their cattle drank, and they sanctified the Lord anyway, despite that great cost.

teachings.title: My presence shall go with thee
teachings.summary: The angel and presence that went before Israel was Christ, the way we can come to the glory of God without being consumed.
teachings.text:
*And I will send an angel before thee; and I will drive out the Canaanite, the Amorite, and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite: Unto a land flowing with milk and honey.*..

This is both a picture of, and literally IMO, Christ Jesus. God with us. Who appears to Moses, face to face even as God says He can't be seen in His full glory. Even as we have God the Father talking about His inaccessibility, the ordinances for the Tabernacle and diverse washings. That Moses will see only His hinder parts, for the glory of God is too much for man to see.

But in Christ Jesus, we are able to go boldly before the Father. The veil of the temple torn. *My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.*

Jesus is the way we can come to the glory of God without being consumed. Amen

teachings.title: Jesus the bread which came down from heaven
teachings.summary: The manna in the wilderness pictures Christ the bread of life, and in John 6 the unbelieving Jews murmured and took His spiritual lesson literally.
teachings.text:
In **Exodus 16** we find the recently freed Isralites, a month now out from bondage in Egypt, shown signs and wonders of God by Moses, murmuring that they were better off in chains. Having run low on supplies, their flesh in need afflicted their spirit.

But God hears their murmurs, and tells Moses and Aaron that he will send them bread to eat in the morning, and the flesh of quails at night. God sets the rules of His heavenly bread that each person takes the measure allotted, and uses it that day, and all would be filled. If they tried to store it up for the next day, it would rot, except for that manna gathered on the day before the sabbath, which would feed them both days.

And like the entire story of Exodus, we have a picture of salvation in Christ.

Jesus, who is the bread of life. Jesus, who is the sabbath. Our rest. Jesus who was sent by God the Father that all who believe on Him shall never hunger. Jesus is the rock from which the water springs as well, as we will soon see. And those that believe on Him shall never thirst.

In **John 6**, Jesus is preaching to the crowd that had followed Him to Capernaum, He had just fed the multitudes with a few loaves and fishes, that thousands were full and there was more to spare. Like in the wilderness of Sin, He fed them whether they followed God's laws or not, to prove them, that they may know He was of God.

But Jesus first chastises the multitude, saying they didn't come to Him for spiritual reasons, but because their belly was full.

And just as the children of Israel in the wilderness murmured against Moses, against God, here too the Bible says they murmured against Christ;

*The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven.*

And Jesus, being God, hears their murmurs and knows their hearts, and says; *Murmur not among yourselves. No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me. Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father. Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life.*
 *I am that bread of life.*

*Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.*

He is giving a spiritual lesson using the allegory of bread from Heaven, the manna in the wilderness, and applying it to His own body, which in death would take on the sins of the world that whoever believes on Him shall have eternal life.

But the unbelieving Jews, unable to understand Jesus take what He says literally and scoff; *The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat?*

And knowing their hardened hearts and dull hearing, Jesus doubles down on His parable;

*Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you. Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.  For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him. As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me;  This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever.*

Get the context; Jesus had just preached a basic parable of salvation in Him, using the manna and Hia miracle the day before, as a picture of the spiritual application of belief and eternal life, and they couldn't understand it.

teachings.title: Joseph's Brothers Hated Him as the Jews Hated Christ
teachings.summary: The brothers' resentment of Joseph's prophetic dreams mirrors the Jews' hatred of Christ, of whom Moses and the prophets wrote.
teachings.text:
And so, we understand the setting. They hate the favoritism Jacob gives his son, Joseph and that he's tattled on their sin. *They hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him*, and to compound matters, Joseph tells them of his dream.

*For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.*
*And his brethren said to him, Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us? And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words.*

In parallel to Christ, we see the resentment. Like Jews resentment of Christians, the older hating the younger because of the prophecy of who will reign. Not exact but echos. And Joseph dreams again.

*And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me. And he told it to his father, and to his brethren: and his father rebuked him, and said unto him, What is this dream that thou hast dreamed? Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth?*

Here Jacob interpreting the dream for us, that he is the sun and his mother, the moon. The brothers the stars. All bowing before Joseph. The brothers hated him even the more, but Jacob observed the saying.

The prophetic dreams about Joseph are from God, given by the Holy Ghost. We will see later how tied to dreams and prophecy Joseph is. But note the building resentment of the brothers mirrors Israel's resentment of Christ, where Jesus speaks to the Jews about how the prophets spoke of Him;

**John 5:46**
*For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me; for he wrote of me.*

**Luke 24:44**
*These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me*

They had the word of the prophets and hated Jesus because of it. In spite of it. Despite the truth of the prophecy being the hope of salvation, they hated the idea of bowing to Christ the Lord.

Joseph's brothers didn't understand that his dream of preeminence was to prophesy their physical salvation.

teachings.title: Jacob wrestled with God face to face
teachings.summary: The man who wrestled Jacob was Christ, who renamed him Israel, a picture of being born again.
teachings.text:
And so, Jacob having prepared his own ways to protect what he has is now alone in the wilderness.

And there, he finds himself wrestling with a man, and there wrestled with him until the breaking of the day.

Jacob, an old man by our standards. Likely 60-70 years old at this point. Having been a rancher for decades, but still not a young man, endures this wrestling all night unto morning. And as the dawn came and the man saw he was in a stalemate with Jacob, touches his thigh and shrinks the sinew of his hip and lames Jacob, and doing this says "Let me go." Essentially telling the exhausted and now hobbled Jacob to give up and surrender. And Jacob defiantly says no, "*I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."*

The man asks, "What is thy name?"

"Jacob."

*And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed*.

*And Jacob asked him, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, thy name. And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name? And he blessed him there. And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.*

The man he'd wrestled with all night was Christ Jesus, God in the flesh. And having overcome, was born again, given a new name. (As Jesus we know is want to do)

Face to face with God, halted and lame for his experience, he is blessed as a prince, inheritor of the blessing, recognizing God come in the flesh. And he passes through the river Penuel, a sort of baptism, the sun rises to warm him, Israel goes to meet his fate.

teachings.title: The Judge of all the earth at Abraham's tent
teachings.summary: Comparing scripture, the Lord who ate with Abraham was Christ, since no man has seen the Father and Jesus is the Judge of all the earth.
teachings.text:
*And the* Lord *appeared unto Abraham.*..This is an Old Testament manifestation of Christ Jesus, appearing with two messengers, angels of the Lord before Abraham on their way to judge Sodom and Gomorrah.

Seeing them approach, Abraham recognizes Him, and runs to prepare a meal, and give hospitality to God and His angels.

We can know this is Jesus, by comparing scripture with scripture. *No man hath seen God at any time, the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.*

But as we have seen repeatedly in the OT, the Lord, the word of God, and here, "Judge of all the earth" appears before Abraham and Sarah, talking with them and eating. Abraham recognizes Him right away.

The Bible says Jesus is the Judge of all the earth.

**Acts 10:42**
*And he commanded us to preach unto the people, and to testify that it is he which was ordained of God to be the Judge of quick and dead.*

**2 Corinthians 5:10**
*For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.*

As the Bible says in James 5, *behold, the Judge is standing right at the door.* Just as He was before the door of the tent of Abraham, on the plains of Mamre, West of Sodom.

There, the Lord reiterated the promise and the blessing to Abraham, that he and Sarah will have a son. That their seed will bless all nations.

We've covered that the seed is singular, Christ Jesus.

Sarah laughs, *After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?* and in a way familiar to us from the Gospels, and recognize in our walk with Him, He calls her on it and when she denies it in shame, He gently chides her, *Nay; but thou didst laugh.*

There is nothing beyond what the Lord can do. *At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.*

teachings.title: God will provide himself a lamb
teachings.summary: Abraham offering Isaac on Moriah pictures God giving His only begotten Son, from the third day and the wood carried up the hill to the ram in the thorns.
teachings.text:
and it came to pass after these things, the god did tempt Abraham, and said unto him, Abraham: and he said, behold, *here I am.* (Remember this for later)

Take thy thou only son whom you lovest, take him to the land of Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1 tells us that Moriah is where Jerusalem is). And offer him there for a burnt offering (Jesus three days and nights in Hell) upon one of the mountains which I will tell the of (Golgotha?)

On the third day, (obvious), Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place a far off. (Jesus lifting up his eyes rising up from hell)

I in the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you. (Abraham had no doubt that even if he slay his son that God would resurrect him).

And Abraham took the wood of the burned offering and laid it upon Isaac his son and he took the fire in his hand in a knife and they went both of them together. (Isaac the sacrifice carrying wood up the hill of Golgotha in Jerusalem)

Behold the fire and wood but where is the Lamb for burnt offering? And Abraham said *God will provide himself* a lamb for burnt offering. (God literally is providing himself as the lamb for the burnt offering. That's carefully phrased don't miss it)

And Abraham stretch for with his hand and the knife to slay his son. And the angel of the Lord called unto him out of heaven, and said, abraham, Abraham: and he said *here am I.* (*Here I am* is where you brought yourself. *Here am I*  is a place where you've been brought)

And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad neither do thou anything unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou has not withheld by son, thine only son from me. (Again.
